newsitem.title: USA: Prince Rupert mayor apologizes for ferry holdup.
newsitem.headline: Prince Rupert mayor apologizes for ferry holdup.

text.p: The mayor of the Canadian port city where an Alaska state ferry was blockaded for three days by angry Canadian fisherman sent a letter of apology on Tuesday to Alaska's governor.

In his letter to Gov. Tony Knowles, Jack Mussallem, mayor of Prince Rupert, British Columbia, called the blockade by hundreds of Canadian fishing vessels "misguided and damaging to the excellent working relationship that has always existed" between the city and the Alaska Marine Highway System.

Mussallem said in the letter that the city council has hired legal counsel to see what steps can be taken "to ensure an immediate and enforceable response to any such future actions, however unlikely."
The mayor said city officials are also seeking to make sure Alaska gets compensated for its financial losses.

After Canadian fishermen barricaded the Alaska ferry in Prince Rupert's harbour on Saturday, the state suspended service there and ceased $16,500-a-month lease payments for the ferry terminal, said Knowles' press secretary Bob King.

The fishermen's protest, which held up the ferry Malaspina and more than 300 passengers, was over alleged Alaskan interception of Canada-bound sockeye salmon. The Canadian fishermen freed the Malaspina late on Monday night.
But future state ferry service to Prince Rupert remained in doubt, with state officials worried about passenger and vessel safety, King said.
The Alaska Marine Highway System is a vital transporation link for southeast Alaska, where almost all communities -- including the state capital of Juneau -- lack road access.

In contrast, Prince Rupert, about 90 miles (145 km) southeast of Ketchikan, Alaska, has access by highway and rail. That makes it a logical stop for the state ferry system, said Tom Garrett, director of the Alaska Division of Tourism.

"Personally, I think Prince Rupert's a pretty good spot for a ferry terminal," he said. But some Alaskans have argued that the Alaska state ferries, each named for a notable Alaska glacier and dubbed "blue canoes" in local lingo, should not stop at any Canadian port, he said.
"There has always been an undercurrent in Alaska to quit going to Prince Rupert," he said.
